extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students in mathematical logic / computability theory
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory-to-intermediate textbook material explaining conditions and constructions used in Godel's incompleteness theorems and the arithmetization of syntax (definitions of theories, representability, provability predicates, and related computability facts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point / self-referential function existence (use of fixed-point lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given computable functions k, l, and m, the fixed-point lemma guarantees a partial computable f satisfying: f(y) ≃ k(y) if l(y) = 0, and f(y) ≃ f(m(y)) otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction: define g(x,y) ≃ k(y) if l(y)=0, else φ_x(m(y)), and use the fixed-point lemma to obtain index e with φ_e(y) = g(e,y). Example: define gcd by a self-referential equation and then prove totality by induction. Note: this is a general method for defining functions in terms of an index for an algorithm computing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Many-one reduction properties (composition and characteristic function behavior)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f is a many-one reduction of A to B, then certain algebraic/characteristic-function relations hold (e.g., χ_A = χ_B ◦ f). Composition: if f reduces A to B and g reduces B to C, then g ∘ f reduces A to C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use composition to chain reductions; check characteristic functions compose as χ_A(x) = χ_B(f(x)). Problems and propositions in the text ask to prove closure under composition and the identity χ_A = χ_B ◦ f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory (closure under entailment)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set of sentences Γ is a theory iff it is closed under entailment, i.e., Γ = {α : Γ ⊨ α}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two common ways to present theories: (1) as the set of sentences true in some structure (e.g., the standard model B), or (2) as the closure under entailment of a specified set of axioms Γ0 (axiomatized theories).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard model of arithmetic (definition of B)
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard model B: domain |B| = N with 0_B = 0, successor ′ interpreted by n↦n+1, + and × interpreted as usual, and < as the standard ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define true arithmetic TA = {α : |=_B α} and to assess truth of LA-sentences; distinguishes between language symbols (×) and their intended interpretation (·).

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory of true arithmetic (TA)
rubrics_metrics.description: TA is the set of sentences satisfied in the standard model B: TA = {α : |=_B α}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TA is complete (settles every sentence in LA) but not axiomatizable; TA contains all arithmetical truths about N expressed in LA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatized theory (Γ axiomatized by Γ0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Γ is axiomatized by Γ0 iff Γ = {α : Γ0 ⊨ α} (Γ is the closure under entailment of the axioms Γ0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An axiomatization is only practically useful if Γ0 is explicitly specified and decidable; many theories of interest (finite axiom sets or schemata like PA) are axiomatized in this sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robinson's Q (axioms Q1–Q8)
rubrics_metrics.description: Q is the theory axiomatized by the eight specific sentences Q1–Q8 (basic properties of 0, successor, +, ×, and <).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Q is a very weak but important theory of arithmetic; it is axiomatizable (finite axioms) and will be shown to represent basic computable functions and relations despite its weakness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction schema and Peano Arithmetic (PA)
rubrics_metrics.description: An instance of the induction schema is any sentence of the form ∀y1...∀yn ((α(0) ∧ ∀x(α(x) → α(x′))) → ∀x α(x)). PA is axiomatized by Q plus all instances of the induction schema.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every instance of induction is true in the standard model; PA is stronger than Q and is a central example of a theory to which incompleteness theorems apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness of a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory Γ is complete iff for every sentence α in its language, either Γ ⊨ α or Γ ⊨ ¬α (equivalently, by the Completeness Theorem, either Γ ⊢ α or Γ ⊢ ¬α).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Completeness can be interpreted semantically (entailment) or syntactically (provability). Completeness of a theory implies decidability when combined with axiomatizability (see Theorem 153B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decidable set (decidability)
rubrics_metrics.description: A set X is decidable iff there is a computational procedure which on input x returns 1 if x ∈ X and 0 otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define decidable theories (membership test for sentences) and decidable axiom sets; decidability of a theory means there is an algorithm answering 'is α ∈ Γ?' for every α.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatizable theory (decidable axioms)
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is axiomatizable iff it is axiomatized by a decidable set of axioms (i.e., the set Γ0 of axioms is decidable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finite or schematically specified axiom sets (like Q or PA's axiom schema) are examples; axiomatizability is one of the conditions appearing in incompleteness theorems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computably enumerable (c.e.) set
rubrics_metrics.description: A set X is computably enumerable (c.e.) iff it is empty or has a computable surjection f : N → X (i.e., X has a computable enumeration).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Axiomatizable theories are c.e. because one can enumerate their theorems by enumerating correct derivations; being c.e. differs from decidable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of functions in a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A wff α(x1,...,xk,y) represents a function f : N^k → N in Γ iff whenever f(n1,...,nk)=m then (1) Γ ⊢ α(n1,...,nk,m) and (2) Γ ⊢ ∀y(α(n1,...,nk,y) → y = m).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Representation ensures the theory proves the function's value exists and is unique for given inputs; essential for expressing computable functions within arithmetic theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representability of relations in a theory
rubrics_metrics.description: A wff α(x1,...,xk) represents a relation R ⊆ N^k in Γ iff (1) whenever R(n1,...,nk) then Γ ⊢ α(n1,...,nk), and (2) whenever not R(n1,...,nk) then Γ ⊢ ¬α(n1,...,nk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full representability of decidable relations means the theory proves membership and non-membership for each tuple; used in diagonal/undecidability arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory 'strong enough' for incompleteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory is 'strong enough' for the incompleteness theorems if it represents all computable functions and all decidable relations (Q and its extensions satisfy this condition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the semantic/computability strength condition in the incompleteness theorems; once Q is shown to represent all recursive functions, any stronger theory inherits this property.

rubrics_metrics.name: First incompleteness theorem applicability condition
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a consistent, axiomatizable theory in LA which represents all computable functions and decidable relations, then Γ is not complete (Theorem 152A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaning: under these conditions there exists a sentence χ_Γ such that Γ ⊬ χ_Γ and Γ ⊬ ¬χ_Γ; the proof constructs a Gödel sentence via arithmetization of syntax and a provability predicate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for arithmetization of syntax (Gödel numbering and computability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Syntactic objects (symbols, terms, wffs, derivations) must be coded as numbers in such a way that properties and operations on them correspond to decidable/computable predicates and functions (typically primitive recursive).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a systematic coding (e.g., prime-power sequence coding) so that length, i-th symbol, well-formedness, and derivation-verification are computable/primitive recursive; this enables expressing syntactic relations in LA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provability predicate Prov_Γ(x) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: There must be a wff Prov_Γ(x) such that if α is coded by n and Γ ⊢ α, then Γ ⊢ Prov_Γ(n) (Prov_Γ expresses 'n is the code of a Γ-provable sentence').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With such a predicate the theory can express its own provability and consistency: e.g., the consistency statement is expressible as ¬Prov_Γ(n) for n coding a contradiction; this is central to the second incompleteness theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undecidability criterion via representability of decidable relations
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is a consistent theory that represents every decidable relation, then Γ is not decidable (Theorem 153A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses a diagonal construction: enumerate wffs α_n(x) representing one-place decidable properties, define D = {n : Γ ⊢ ¬α_n(n)} which is decidable under the false assumption that Γ is decidable, derive contradiction from representability of D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiomatizable + complete implies decidable
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is axiomatizable and complete (and consistent), then Γ is decidable (Theorem 153B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerate theorems of Γ; since Γ is complete, either α or ¬α will appear, so membership in Γ is decidable. This fact is used together with Theorem 153A to derive incompleteness corollaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: consistent, axiomatizable, and representing decidable properties implies incompleteness
rubrics_metrics.description: If Γ is consistent, axiomatizable, and represents every decidable property, then Γ is not complete (Corollary 153C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combines previous theorems: axiomatizable+complete⇒decidable, but representing all decidable properties ⇒ not decidable; hence such Γ cannot be complete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example exception: Presburger arithmetic (decidable and complete)
rubrics_metrics.description: Presburger arithmetic (theory of natural numbers without ×, i.e., language with 0, ′, +) is both decidable and complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as an example showing that incompleteness/undecidability do not hold for every sufficiently interesting theory; the presence or absence of multiplication (×) can change decidability properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that a theory prove basic facts about computable functions
rubrics_metrics.description: A theory meant to formalize arithmetic must be able to prove basic arithmetical facts (e.g., Q proves concrete equations like (2+3)=5) and, more generally, must be able to represent computable functions so that Γ ⊢ α_f(n1,...,nk,m) when f(n1,...,nk)=m.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is necessary so that arithmetization and provability predicates behave as required; demonstrating Q's ability to represent recursive functions is a technical but central task in the development.
